content: The alkaline earth metals are a group of elements that belong to Group 2 of the periodic table, as defined by IUPAC. This group includes beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg), calcium (Ca), strontium (Sr), barium (Ba), and radium (Ra). These elements exhibit clear periodic trends in their chemical and physical properties, demonstrating homologous behavior as one moves down the group. Alkaline earth metals are silvery in appearance and are relatively soft. They react readily with halogens to form ionic salts and with water to produce strongly alkaline hydroxides. However, their reactivity with water is less vigorous compared to the alkali metals. For instance, while sodium and potassium react with water at room temperature, magnesium reacts only with steam, and calcium reacts with hot water. Beryllium is an exception in this group, as it does not react with water or steam, and its halides are covalent in nature. All alkaline earth metals have two electrons in their outermost electron shell. To achieve a stable electronic configuration, they tend to lose these two electrons, forming doubly charged positive ions (cations). The name alkaline earth metals originates from their oxides, historically referred to as alkaline earths, which include beryllia, magnesia, lime, strontia, and baryta. These oxides are basic (alkaline) when combined with water. The term earth was used by early chemists to describe nonmetallic substances that were insoluble in water and resistant to heat, properties shared by these oxides. Antoine Lavoisier was the first to recognize that these earths were not elements but compounds. In his 1789 work Traité Élémentaire de Chimie (Elements of Chemistry), he referred to them as salt-forming earth elements. Later, he hypothesized that these alkaline earths might be metal oxides, though he admitted this was speculative. In 1808, Humphry Davy, building on Lavoisier's ideas, successfully isolated the metals from their molten oxides using electrolysis. Biological Occurrences Beryllium has very low solubility in aqueous environments, making it rarely available to biological systems. It has no known biological role and is highly toxic when encountered by living organisms. Magnesium and calcium, on the other hand, are essential to all known forms of life and are ubiquitous in biological systems. For example, calcium is a critical component of bones and teeth, while magnesium plays a vital role in numerous enzymatic processes. Strontium and barium have much lower availability in the biosphere and generally do not play natural roles in biological systems. A rare exception is the primitive marine organism Acantharea, which incorporates strontium sulfate into its exoskeleton. Despite their limited biological roles, these elements have some medical applications. For instance, barium is used in barium meals for radiographic imaging, and strontium compounds are included in certain toothpaste formulations. Radium, due to its high radioactivity and low availability, is highly toxic to living organisms and has no biological role.
